title: Not touching the clarinet; musicians who stop playing
summary: He hasn't played in years; they discuss loss of technique and George Mitchell refusing to play.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Lips, teeth and breath: the physical craft of brass playing

blocks.x: You say that you haven't been playing for a long time, right?
No, I haven't actually touched the clarinet for a couple of years now.
Well, did it have something to do with being busy or being satisfied or not having work?

Well, I would like... I think sometimes that I would like to play and you pick up the clarinet and your fingers don't move as fast as they used to and your lip gets tired and so you get discouraged and you put it away and you don't touch it again for a long time. And so every time you pick it up it works, so eventually you just stop altogether. Too fresh, isn't it? Yes, yeah. That's one of those things you have to keep at it constantly or else you lose touch with it.

Well, so many people who drop out of music find an opportunity to play once in a while and decide that they, oh, we'll forget the loss of technique forgetfulness of tunes and so forth. Yeah. Well, you just go ahead and try. Yeah. And I know that they feel somewhat disappointed with their performance. Yeah. Others are so disappointed and I think that maybe they were a little tense in their original endeavors. that they were so devoted that they can't stand that disappointment. George Mitchell is one of those. Oh. George has refused for 20 years to play publicly. Yeah. Yet, when I called on him the last time his music rack was up. Oh, yeah. As if he'd been reading. So, so. But he refused to play. How old is he now? I'd guess in the 70s. Mm-hmm. Franz Jackson invited him to play when Bob Schaffner was ill. Mm-hmm. And, well, maybe he would. But he says maybe I think instead of saying no. Yeah. Yeah. He means no. Because he has it. And, uh, uh, there are several who, uh, can't get over the fact that they are losing touch with their peak performance and they can't count on doing less than their best.
